title: The State of Hotel Missed Calls
summary: At least 52.7% of DACH hotels show phone-reachability friction. Live traffic at one busy property: 71% of front-desk calls unanswered. Original 2026 data, methods, and limits.
body_markdown:
Common questions


## FAQ


### Do hotels really miss phone calls?


Yes, and the evidence is not one study. In an enrichment of 26,707 hotels in Germany, Austria and Switzerland with live websites (June 2026), at least 52.7% showed one or more detectable phone or reachability friction signals, 14,075 hotels. That is a floor, because detection only catches what a hotel's own website reveals. Live call traffic is the harder check: at one high-volume property handling more than 300 calls, 71% of front-desk calls went unanswered over 31 days. A second busy property sat at roughly 40% answered and 60% missed. Most hotels have no report that would show them this, which is why the objection "we don't miss calls" survives.


### How many reservations do hotels lose to missed calls?


Nobody can count the reservations that never happened. What can be sized is the booking intent on the line. In a three-month analysis across 59 hotels and more than 80,000 calls, roughly one in five engaged calls (about 20.9%) was someone trying to make a new room booking. Separately, a city hotel of around 200 rooms takes on the order of 700 to 800 calls a month. Those two ranges come from different samples and should not be multiplied into a fake annual total. They are enough to say the leak is demand, not only service. For hotels without a real online booking engine (only 54.2% of the DACH universe run one), a missed call is often a missed reservation attempt on the channel the hotel itself uses to take bookings.


### We have 24/7 reception. Does this apply to us?


The most common website signal is no 24/7 reception, at 27.9% of hotels. If you do staff around the clock, that particular signal is not yours. The rest of the picture can still be. Live no-pickup at busy properties is a handling problem, not a roster problem: one high-volume desk left 71% of calls unanswered over 31 days. Digitally mature groups, the ones that already look current on the web, still carry material phone friction in 58% of cases. Fixing the website does not fix the phone. A 24/7 roster means someone is in the building. It does not mean the ringing phone is the thing they can drop.


### How was this data collected?


Three layers. A website-signal scan of 26,707 DACH hotels with live websites, June 2026, using eight reachability tags and reporting every prevalence as a lower bound. A review check of about 11,700 recent booking-platform reviews across about 376 hotels. Live call-handling data on properties with more than 300 calls in a 31-day window. Full definitions, sample limits, and the things this report does not claim are in the methodology section above.


### Where does the data come from?


Germany, Austria and Switzerland. The core universe is 26,707 hotels with a live website, enriched in June 2026 (export 28 June 2026). Review samples were scraped on 9 and 10 July 2026 from booking-platform listings covering about 73% of that list. Live no-pickup rates are from call-handling records at high-volume properties, not from the website scan. Operators outside DACH should read the pattern as transferable and the exact percentages as DACH-specific.
